title: Setup
text:
This workshop uses the community version of Beekeeper Studio for the simplicity of its user interface, which makes it easy for beginners to foucs on learning SQL syntax and relational database structure without being overwhelmed by the features intended for database administators available in commercial database management software.
Once you’ve learned a little SQL, I would encourage you to branch out to a more powerful tool. The final lesson in this workshop will introduce alternatives that are free to users with a university affiliation. There are differences in SQL dialects, but almost everything you learn in this workshop can be translated to a different SQL engine or different database management system.

title: Setup
text:
Install Beekeeper Studio Community Edition

MacOS
Depending on when you bought your laptop, your Mac may have an Apple Silicon chip or an Intel Chip. For Beekeeper Studio to work correctly, you must install the version that corresponds to your laptop’s chip.

Identify Your Processor Type

Click on the Apple icon in the top left corner of your screen.
Select About this Mac.
Look at the line labeled Chip.


If your chip name begins with Apple, it is an Apple Silicon processor.
If your chip name begins with Intel, it is an Intel processor.



Download and Install Beekeeper Studio

Go to beekeeper-studio.io
Click Download.
Click Skip to the download.
Download the Mac app version that corresponds to your processor type to your Desktop.
Navigate to your Desktop and double-click the .dmg file.
A window will prompt you to drag the Beekeeper Studio app to your Applications folder.
Use Go->Applications to open your Applications folder.
Click Beekeeper Studio.app.




Windows

Go to beekeeper-studio.io
Click Download.
Click Skip to the download.
Download the Windows Installer to your Desktop.
Run the .exe installer.
When prompted, choose to install the application only for you.
After the installer finishes, you will be prompted to launch Beekeeper Studio.


In the future, you can launch the program from the Windows Start Menu.

title: Setup
section: Download the Sample Database: The “Chinook” Music Store
text:
Download the Sample Database: The “Chinook” Music Store
Real-world relational databases are typically run on a server, a continously running computer accessible by many users or programs simultaneously. However, for teaching purposes, we will be using a lightweight database format called SQLite. SQLite is a program that can read (and write) a database to a specially formatted file stored on your computer. SQLite is used in mobile apps and other smart devices to store and manage data because it is simple, portable, and compact.



A diagram of the workshop technical stack


The Chinook database represents purchase records for a digital media store, including tables for artists, albums, media tracks, invoices and customers. Think of it as a miniature version of the iTunes Music Store. While the names of the bands and albums in the dataset are real, the purchase information is completely fictional. This dataset is popular for teaching because it’s open-source, demonstrates good database design principles, and gives students the opportunity to practice a variety of SQL features.
SQLite requires a .sqlite file to run, so you will need to save this file somewhere in a location you can remember.
Make a new folder named SQLWorkshop in your Documents folder or on your Desktop. Keep track of this folder for the duration of the workshop.
Click the button below to download a copy of the Chninook database to your computer. Save or copy the file to your SQLWorkshop folder.
 Download Database File

title: Setup
section: Import the Sample Database into Beekeeper Studio
text:
Import the Sample Database into Beekeeper Studio



The launch screen of Beekeeper Studio


Now that you have the database file stored in your SQLWorkshop, launch Beekeeper Studio. You will be prompted to create a new database connection.
Select SQLite from the Connection Type drop-down menu. Then, click the Choose File button and select the Chinook_Sqlite.sqilte file inside your SQLWorkshop folder. Give your connection a name you can remember, like Chinook.



A connection configuration for Beekeeper Studio


Once you’ve completed these steps, click the Test button. If the connection succeeds, click the Connect button.






TipNeed Help?



If the connection test fails, please raise your hand or type in the Zoom chat. Someone will help you troubleshoot your configuration.

title: Setup
text:
Optional: Configure Beekeeper Studio
Congratulations! You’re now set up to do this workshop. If you would like to tailor Beekeeper Studio to your preferences, you can adjust its appearance by going to View -> Theme in the top menu bar.

title: Selection Fundamentals
text:
You might have noticed that I’ve been entering each clause in these SQL queries in a specific order. SELECT comes before FROM which comes before LIMIT. This is because the grammar of SQL requires keywords to have a hierarchy and order. We will discuss the syntactic placement of each keyword as new ones are introduced.
As an example, let’s see what happens if we invert the order of SELECT and FROM in a query.
FROM Customer
SELECT Email
LIMIT 5;
near "FROM": syntax error
If you get a syntax error message when running a query, inspect the grammar of your query carefully.
The SELECT keyword must be followed by a * or the name or one or more columns in the table in the FROM clause. If you ask SQL to select a column that doesn’t exist, the query will fail.
SELECT email_address
FROM CUSTOMER
LIMIT 5;
no such column: email_address - Check that you only use double 
quotes (") for identifiers, not strings
When you see a no such column error message, check the spelling the name of each field in the SELECT clause. Remember you can use the Entity pane on the left side of Beekeeper Studio or the name and data type of each column in your database at any time; make sure the name matches exactly.


We may want to sort the results of a query by a particular column. We can do this in SQL by adding an ORDER BY clause to our query.
ORDER BY must followed by the name of one or more columns, and the ORDER BY clause always comes just before LIMIT.
SELECT *
FROM Artist
ORDER BY Name
LIMIT 3;

title: Selection Fundamentals
text:
Filtering with WHERE
So far, we have written queries that isolate specific columns from a table without consideration to which rows are returned.
The SQL WHERE clause gives us the ability to filter results to records with values that fit specific criteria. The WHERE clause is always followed by a conditional statement, something that can be evaluated as True or False.

SQL has six available logical operators: =, <, <=, >=, >, and !=. = is a test for equality, and != means “not equal to”.

For example, the following query returns the CustomerId and Total from the rows of the Invoice table which Total was greater than $20.00.
SELECT CustomerId, Total
FROM Invoice
WHERE Total > 20;



CustomerId
Total




45
21.86


46
21.86


26
23.86


6
25.86



The following query returns all the tracks in the Track table with the value Carlos Santana in the Composer field.
SELECT TrackId, Name, Composer
FROM Track 
WHERE Composer = 'Carlos Santana';

Name

Important



Valid strings in SQL must use single quotes. When writing WHERE clauses, use strings in the form 'value', not "value".


The database manager executes this query in two stages. First, it checks at each row in the Track table to see which ones have a Composer equal to 'Carlos Santana'. Then, it uses the column names following the SELECT keyword to determine which columns to display.
This ordering means we can filter records using WHERE based on values in columns that aren’t displayed.
SELECT TrackId
From Track
Where Composer = 'Carlos Santana'

SELECT CustomerId, Total, InvoiceDate
FROM Invoice
WHERE InvoiceDate < '2021-01-05' -- Dates are in YYYY-MM-DD order!
ORDER BY InvoiceDate DESC;

Pattern Matching with LIKE
Textual data is complicated. We often want to retrieve approximate matches in a WHERE clause because of the messy nature of textual values like descriptions, names, and titles.
For example, when we looked for tracks composed by Carlos Santana in the Track table, we could only retrieve songs with precisely the value 'Carlos Santata', a choice that excludes collaborations in forms like 'R. Taha, Carlos Santana & T. Lindsay'.
We can use the LIKE keyword to express fuzzy matching. Remember that a character can be a space, letter, or even a symbol.

% - matches any characters of length 0 or more
_ - matches any one character

Let’s rewrite our first WHERE query to capture Carlos Santana’s collaborative efforts.
SELECT Name, Composer
FROM Track
WHERE Composer LIKE '%Carlos Santana%'
ORDER BY Composer;

Keep in mind that, by default, patterns with letters in SQLite are case-insensitive. The pattern '%And%' matches both Andy and Cat and Dog.

Quiz: Wildcard Practice
Which of the following patterns would match the string 'Sandwich' if used with LIKE in a WHERE clause?

 Sa%witch Sandwi__ '_Sandwich'



Caveat: Escape Characters
SQL strings are always wrapped in single-quotes. This is unfortunate when we want to express words that contain conjuctions like the words can't or don't.
Let’s say I want to find the first five songs (in alphabetical order) in the database that begin with the word Don't.
A naive attempt would look something like this: it produces a syntax error.
SELECT Name
FROM Track
WHERE Name LIKE 'Don't %'
ORDER BY Name
LIMIT 5;
near "t": syntax error
We need to tell SQL that the apostrophe in Don't is part of the pattern. To do this, use a second apostrophe to escape the quote.
SELECT Name
FROM Track
WHERE Name LIKE 'Don''t %'
ORDER BY Name
LIMIT 5;



Name




Don’t Cry


Don’t Cry (Original)


Don’t Damn Me


Don’t Forget Me


Don’t Go Away Mad (Just Go Away)

About
This interactive workshop teaches the fundamentals of using SQL (Structured Query Language) to extract and analyze data from relational databases. Learn how to sort, filter, aggregation, and join data with SQL by writing your own queries!
No experience with SQL required, though participants may benefit from familiarity with programming languages like R or Python.

title: Intermediate Selection
text:
What if we want to express something more complicated in the WHERE clause? For example, how do we filter rows that require conditions to be fulfilled by multiple fields?
We can use the logical operators OR, AND, and NOT to combine conditions in our WHERE clause. Use parantheses to express to SQL how you want these conditions to be combined.

(COND 1) AND (COND 2) will return only rows where both COND1 and COND2 are true.
(COND 1) OR (COND 2) will return only rows where either COND1 or COND2 are true.
NOT(COND 1) will return only rows where COND1 is false.

The following query returns all the tracks that begin with the word Love and have a file size larger than 10MB, or 10000000 bytes.
SELECT Name, Bytes
FROM Track
WHERE (Name LIKE 'Love%') AND (Bytes > 10000000);

title: Intermediate Selection
text:
What About NULL?
NULL is a special value in SQL to indicate that something is not complete. It is not zero, and isn’t a bad thing.
Null values can represent values that may be:

undefined
unknown
unapplicable

Take the Customer table. Some customers have a known company affiliation in the Company field, but not every customer could be expected to have a business. What about unemployed customers? Or users who simply chose not to provide where they work? For those rows, a NULL value makes the most sense.
SELECT CustomerId, LastName, Company 
FROM Customer 
LIMIT 3;








CustomerId
LastName
Company




1
Gonçalves
Embraer - Empresa Brasileira de Aeronáutica S.A.


2
Köhler
null


3
Tremblay
null




Using IS NULL and NOT NULL
You can’t identify null values in the WHERE clause using = or != because null is not equal to (or equal to) any real value.
SELECT FirstName, Company
FROM Customer
WHERE Company=NULL
LIMIT 3;
Query 1/1: No results. 0 rows affected.
The query above gives misleading results. From a manual inspection of the table in the Beekeeper Studio data tab, we can see that plenty of rows have NULL for the company attribute.
Instead, we identify NULL values in the WHERE using is NULL and is not NULL.
SELECT FirstName, Company
FROM Customer
WHERE Company is NULL
LIMIT 3;



FirstName
Company




Leonie
null


François
null


Bjørn
null



Null values are never included when filtering with the comparatives (<, =, etc. ) we’ve learned so far.
If you’re using a WHERE clause with a comparative operator and do want to include NULL values in your set, use IS NULL and OR.
SELECT FirstName, Company
FROM Customer
WHERE (Company NOT LIKE 'Apple%') OR (Company is NULL)
LIMIT 3;



FirstName
Company




Luís
Embraer - Empresa Brasileira de Aeronáutica S.A.


Leonie
null


François
null





Debugging Practice: I Don’t Want These Nulls!
You have a colleague who wants to find the first five companies in your customer dataset in alphabetical order. When running the following query, they get only nulls in their results. How can they fix it?
SELECT Company
FROM Customer
ORDER BY Company
LIMIT 5;



Company




null

TipAnswer





When sorting NVARCHAR (string) fields in ascending order, null values always come first. However, your colleague is interested in non-null values. Add the WHERE clause to narrow this query.
SELECT Company
FROM Customer
WHERE Company is NOT NULL
ORDER BY Company
LIMIT 5;

title: Intermediate Selection
text:
Using SQL Functions with SELECT
We can now retrieve values from relational database tables with a lot of flexibility, but what about manipulating them? SQL has a number of aggregation functions that collapse one or more values into a single value.

AVG() - average value
MIN() - minimum value
MAX() - max value
COUNT() - the number of values
SUM() - the sum of a set of values

Let’s start with the task of computing the largest Total in the Invoice table. You learned a way to compute this with sorting, but we the same result more effeciently using MAX().
SELECT MAX(Total)
FROM Invoice;



MAX(Total)




25.86



MIN() can be used the same way, and it is compatible with both numeric and textual (varchar) fields.
SELECT MIN(FirstName)
FROM Customer;



MIN(FirstName)




Aaron



Using COUNT(*) in queries without a WHERE clause computes the number of rows in the results. Using COUNT(field_name) computes the number of non-null values for that particular field.
This query gives the total number of rows in Track.
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM Track;



COUNT(*)




3503



COUNT(*) can also be used as shorthand to return the number of rows for which a WHERE clause is TRUE.
For example, this query returns how many customers have no associated Company, that is where Company is null.
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM Customer
WHERE Company is NULL;



COUNT(*)




49



Aggregation in SQL always happens after filtering, so it can be used in combination with the WHERE clause to get aggregated values over a specific subset of rows.
Let’s compute the average value of Total for Invoices with the BillingCountry of Germany.
SELECT AVG(Total)
FROM Invoice
WHERE BillingCountry='Germany';



AVG(Total)




5.588571428571428



Say we want to find the total revenue of our music store in March 2022. That means we need to sum the Total for all rows in the Invoice with an InvoiceDate between March 1st and March 31st.
SELECT SUM(Total)
FROM Invoice
WHERE (InvoiceDate >= '2022-03-01') AND (InvoiceDate <= '2022-03-31');



SUM(Total)




44.62




Quiz: Counting Rows with Filters
Write a query that counts the number of rows in the Customer table in which FirstName begins with the letter F.
Challenge: Write a query that counts the number of rows in the Customer table in which FirstName begins with the letter F and is exactly five letters long.






TipAnswer





SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM Customer
WHERE FirstName LIKE 'F%';



COUNT(*)




6



The challenge answer is as follows.
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE FirstName LIKE 'F____';



COUNT(*)




2








Using AS in the SELECT Clause
Have you noticed the COUNT(*) in our results looks messy? A client might prefer a result that says something Sum or Total or even MonthlyRevenue instead.
SQL allows you to rename attributes (or even tables) on the fly using aliases. Let’s say we want to the compute the sum of all Total values from the Invoice table.
SELECT SUM(Total)
FROM Invoice



SUM(Total)




2328.6



Using AS, we can give our output a temporary name.
SELECT SUM(Total) AS TotalRevenue
FROM Invoice;



TotalRevenue




2328.6



Notice that the numeric result of the query didn’t actually change, only how SQL represented it to us. The table itself didn’t change either.s


Simple Math and Concatenation in SQL
Mathematical operations like addition, multiplication, and division by numerical constants can be performed within the SELECT clause, provided they can be applied to all values in the column.

* multiplication
/ division
+ addition
- subtraction

In the query below, we divide the length of each song in milliseconds by 60000 with /, giving us the length of the song in minutes. Then, we use an alias to give the result the name LengthMinutes.
SELECT Name, Milliseconds/60000.0 as LengthMinutes
FROM Track
LIMIT 3;



Name
LengthMinutes




For Those About To Rock (We Salute You)
5.72865


Balls to the Wall
5.709366666666667


Fast As a Shark
3.84365



The mathematical operators above should only be used with numeric columns. SQLite will not error out, but it will perform undesirable or unexpected behaviors.
If you are interested in manipulating fields with textual data types varchar, consider concatenation. The string concatenation operator || combines strings from left to right.
SELECT Name || ' another string' AS Concatenated
FROM Track

title: Introduction
text:
Technically, any collection of structured information, whether a spreadsheet or set of files, can be considered a database. However, this class will focus on a specific family of databases: relational databases. Relational databases organize information into tables. They have been a fixture of businesses, non-profits, and educational institutions for decades.
Databases grew out of a need for secure, robust, and concurrently accessible records. Databases allow administrators to restrict which users can read, write, or delete information on a table by table basis. For example, at an educational institution like the University of Oregon, it is important that students see their own information but not information pertaining to other students.
We will not get into the details of how databases are managed in this workshop, but it is important to understand that SQL (as a query language) works independently of the implementation of the database. Despite advances in computing technology, many databases still retain the tabular structure popularized in the 80s and 90s.

title: Introduction
text:
Relational Databases: Tables





A relational database stores information in tables or entities. Each table has a set of columns and a variable number of records.

Attributes

Each attribute (also known as a field or column) has an associated data type. You will encounter the following SQL data types in this workshop:

integer: a signed whole number
numeric: used for storing decimals or floats
varchar(n)/nvarchar(n): a string (text) of at most n characters, including spaces
char(n): a string (text) of exactly n characters, including spaces
datetime: a date and time string in the form 'YYYY-MM-DD 00:00:00'

Every value within that column must be of the specified data type, or (when-permitted) NULL.



Records

Every record or row has the same number of attributes.
There is no limit on the number of records in a table. However, for performance reasons, SQL tables should be no larger than they need to be to store required information.

text:
Exploring the Database in Beekeeper Studio

The Beekeeper Studio Interface



The Beekeeper Studio interface


On the left side of Beekeeper Studio, there is a navigation pane with three icons.

The first, a database symbol, allows you to inspect the structure and properties of the current database.
The second allows you to see your saved queries. We’ll talk about saving queries shortly.
Finally, the third allows you to see all the queries you’ve run in the current workspace, including ones you may not have saved.

title: Introduction
text:
SELECT, FROM, and LIMIT
For our first query, let’s list the first and last names of each customer known to have purchased music from the store. To do this, we need the keywords SELECT and FROM.
Click the + button in the Beekeeper Studio editor pane to open a new query console and type the following.



A first query in the Beekepeer Studio console



Unpacking a First SQL Query
SELECT FirstName, LastName 
FROM Customer;

FROM is the most important part of the query. It must be followed by the name of a table in the database.
SELECT is followed by comma-separated names of fields within that table.
Every SQL query ends with a semicolon ;.







Note



SQL is case-insensitive, but it’s best practice to capitalize keywords like SELECT and FROM. It makes it easier to distinguish between keywords and values, which are typically camel case or title case.


To change the order of columns in our ourput, we can rewrite the order as follows:
SELECT LastName, FirstName
FROM Customer;
As a shortcut, we can select all of the columns in a table using *:
SELECT *
FROM Customer;
The * symbol tells SQL to display all of the fields in the table from left to right.


Controlling Output with LIMIT
The Customer table has 59 rows, which is more than we want to read at once. Luckily, SQL has keyword that limits the number of rows returned.
At the end of any SQL command, just before the semicolon, use the keyword LIMIT followed by a number of rows to indicate how many rows we want to return.

LIMIT must be followed by a positive integer.

SELECT LastName, FirstName
FROM Customer
LIMIT 5;
